Withdraw
with-DRAW
v.
From with in its older sense of away or against, and draw. Webster 1828: to take back; to recall; to retire; to retreat. Paul uses it for the church’s ordinary discipline of a disorderly brother, and Proverbs uses it for the plain wisdom of not wearing out a welcome.

Biblical Definition

Withdraw is the New Testament’s word for a measured separation. The command in Thessalonica is explicit and is issued with apostolic authority: we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us (2 Thessalonians 3:6). The offence in that chapter is idleness and busybodying, not heresy, and the aim is stated a few verses later — that he may be ashamed. Yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother. The withdrawal is corrective and it stops short of excommunication. Paul gives the same instruction to Timothy concerning teachers who suppose that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself (1 Timothy 6:5). Proverbs supplies the everyday form of the same wisdom: Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee (Proverbs 25:17). And the word has a solemn use in the other direction, of God withdrawing: Hezekiah was left of God to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart, and the psalmist pleads, Why withdrawest thou thy hand?

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WITHDRAW as to take back; to take from; to recall; to cause to retire or leave; and intransitively, to retire, to retreat, to quit a company or place. The prefix with here carries its ancient sense of away or back.

expand to see more

WITHDRAW, v.t. — To take back; to take from; to recall; as, to withdraw a claim or an accusation.

To cause to retire or leave; to remove; as, to withdraw a garrison from a fort.

WITHDRAW, v.i. — To retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place; to go away.

The prefix is with in the older sense of away or back, as in withhold, withstand, and the obsolete withsay.

The English noun withdrawing room, contracted to drawing room, preserves the same sense of retiring apart.

Key Scripture

2 Thessalonians 3:6 — "Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us."

1 Timothy 6:5 — "Perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself."

Proverbs 25:17 — "Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee."

1 Corinthians 5:11 — "But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat."

Matthew 18:15 — "Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother."

Modern Corruption

Church discipline has been almost entirely abandoned in the modern church, and 2 Thessalonians 3:6 is the text that shows how far the abandonment goes: even the mildest degree of it, over a matter as ordinary as idleness, is a command.

expand to see more

The Reformers named discipline as one of the marks of a true church alongside the preaching of the word and the right administration of the sacraments, and the reason is visible in these texts. Scripture prescribes a graduated response: private admonition (Matthew 18:15), then witnesses, then the church; withdrawal from the disorderly (2 Thessalonians 3:6); refusal of table fellowship with the unrepentant professor (1 Corinthians 5:11); and finally putting away from among yourselves that wicked person. Modern congregations have largely kept the first step in theory and abandoned all the rest, with the result that membership means nothing and the unrepentant are confirmed in their sin by the silence of the people who love them least effectively.

The corruption runs in the other direction too, and it is uglier where it occurs. Paul’s controls are as clear as his command: count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother; restore such an one in the spirit of meekness, considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted; and the whole aim is that he may be ashamed and repent, not that he may be destroyed. Where discipline is exercised without those controls it becomes the shunning of an offender for the comfort of the offended, and Paul’s word for a man restored in 2 Corinthians 2 is that the church should confirm your love toward him lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Discipline that cannot end in restoration was never the biblical thing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek stello (G4724), to draw in, to shrink from, at 2 Thessalonians 3:6; aphistemi (G868), to stand away from, at 1 Timothy 6:5; Hebrew yaqar (H3365) in the proverb, to make rare.

expand to see more

Greek stello (G4724) — to set, to draw in, to avoid; withdraw yourselves (2 Thessalonians 3:6).

Greek aphistemi (G868) — to stand off, to depart from; from such withdraw thyself (1 Timothy 6:5).

Greek ataktos (G814) — disorderly, out of rank; a military word for a soldier out of formation.

Greek entrepo (G1788) — to turn upon oneself, to be ashamed; the stated aim of the withdrawal (2 Thessalonians 3:14).

Hebrew yaqar (H3365) — to be precious, to make rare; literally make thy foot rare in thy neighbour’s house (Proverbs 25:17).

Usage

"Withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly (2 Thessalonians 3:6) — discipline commanded for idleness."

"From such withdraw thyself (1 Timothy 6:5) — separation from teachers who make merchandise of godliness."

"Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house (Proverbs 25:17) — the same wisdom in ordinary manners."
